about: THE GOODS OF 793-1066 - everything a merchant of the time could buy and sell in this world, as a table the game reads (edit freely). Each good: id; name; period (its names then, where known); cat (category); unit (how it was traded) and kg (one unit's weight); bulk (hold space per kg: 1 dense ... 4 light and bulky); value (silver pennies - deniers of about 1.7 g after Charlemagne's reform of 793/4 - for one unit where it is neither made nor wanted: A STARTING GUESS TO TUNE); keeps (days before it spoils; 0 = it keeps); from/to (years it is traded; 0 = always / no end); made and wanted (trade regions with a strength: made 3 = the main source, cheap and plenty, 2, 1, 0.5 = brought in, scarce and dear; wanted 3 = keenly wanted, 2, 1); season (and cheap and dear: the months it is cheapest and dearest); risk; law (arms, captives, sacred, horses: what the realms' laws and the Church forbid, by realm, in trade_rules) (the law and the Church on it); note (plain facts); src (sources, listed below). Regions without ports yet (the Caliphate, Byzantium, Iceland...) matter when their ports come; their goods reach the north at the hubs marked 0.5.

regions.rhine_delta: The Rhine delta: Dorestad, Utrecht, the Betuwe, the IJssel
regions.zeeland: The Scheldt and Maas mouths: Walcheren
regions.frisia: Frisia: the terp country from West Frisia to the Ems
regions.rhineland: The Rhineland: Cologne, Mainz, the Eifel's Mayen
regions.meuse: The Meuse valley: Maastricht, Huy, Dinant
regions.neustria: Neustria: Paris and Saint-Denis, the Seine, Rouen, Quentovic
regions.loire: The Loire and the Bay: Nantes, Noirmoutier's salt
regions.england_east: East Anglia and the Fens: Ipswich
regions.dalriata: Dal Riata and the Isles: Iona
regions.prussia: The Prussians: Truso, the amber coast
regions.norway_north: Halogaland and the Sami: furs, walrus, (later) stockfish
regions.ladoga: Ladoga: Aldeigjuborg, the gate to the east
regions.rus_volga: The Volga: the Bulgars, the furs of the north east
regions.provence: Provence and the Rhone: Marseille, Arles

sources.mccormick2001: McCormick, M. (2001). Origins of the European Economy: Communications and Commerce AD 300-900. Cambridge UP.
sources.verhulst2002: Verhulst, A. (2002). The Carolingian Economy. Cambridge UP.
sources.hodges1982: Hodges, R. (1982). Dark Age Economics: The Origins of Towns and Trade AD 600-1000. Duckworth.
sources.lebecq1983: Lebecq, S. (1983). Marchands et navigateurs frisons du haut Moyen Age. Presses universitaires de Lille.
sources.sawyer2013: Sawyer, P. (2013). The Wealth of Anglo-Saxon England. Oxford UP.
sources.skre2008: Skre, D. (ed.) (2008). Means of Exchange: Dealing with Silver in the Viking Age (Kaupang Excavation Project 2). Aarhus UP.
sources.noonan1998: Noonan, T. S. (1998). The Islamic World, Russia and the Vikings, 750-900: The Numismatic Evidence. Ashgate.
sources.willemsen2010: Willemsen, A. & Kik, H. (eds.) (2010). Dorestad in an International Framework. Brepols.
sources.feveile2006: Feveile, C. (ed.) (2006). Ribe Studier: Det aeldste Ribe. Jysk Arkaeologisk Selskab.
sources.lexrib: Lex Ribuaria, tit. 40 (36): values of a sword, byrnie, helmet, horse, cattle (7th c., in use under the Carolingians).
sources.frankfurt794: Capitulary of Frankfurt (794), c. 4: the public prices of oats, barley, rye and wheat, and of bread.
sources.arms: Capitularies of Herstal (779, c. 20: no byrnies sold out of the realm), Thionville (805, c. 7: no weapons or mail to the Slavs and Avars), Edict of Pitres (864, c. 25: death for selling arms or horses to the Northmen).
sources.raffelstetten: The Raffelstetten customs regulation (c. 903-906): tolls on salt, slaves, horses on the Danube.
sources.ohthere: Ohthere's account of the north, in the Old English Orosius (c. 890): walrus ivory, ship-ropes of hide, the Sami's tribute of furs, feathers and whale bone.
sources.ibnfadlan: Ibn Fadlan, Risala (922): the Rus on the Volga, their trade in slaves and sable.
sources.ibnkh: Ibn Khurradadhbih, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (c. 870): the Rus merchants' furs and swords; the Radhanites' goods.
sources.sindbaek: Sindbaek, S. M. (2007). Networks and nodal points: the emergence of towns in early Viking Age Scandinavia. Antiquity 81.
sources.coupland: Coupland, S. (2005-): on Carolingian coinage and Frisian trade.
sources.barrett2008: Barrett, J. et al. (2008). Detecting the medieval cod trade. Journal of Archaeological Science 35 (stockfish from c. 1000).
sources.ashby2015: Ashby, S. et al. (2015). Urban networks and Arctic outlands: craft specialists and reindeer antler in Viking towns. European Journal of Archaeology 18.
sources.kirk: Kirk, R. and others on Mayen basalt quern exports (Rhineland lava quernstones in the North Sea world).

goods.name: Wheat
goods.unit: sack (about a modius and a half)
goods.season: Cheapest after the harvest (Aug-Oct); dear before it, dearest in a hungry spring
goods.note: Bread corn of the Frankish heartland. In 794 the king fixed the public price of a modius at 4 pennies.

goods.name: Rye
goods.note: The sandy uplands' grain: the Saxons' and the Wends' bread. 3 pennies a modius in 794.

goods.name: Barley
goods.note: For ale and porridge. 2 pennies a modius in 794.

goods.name: Oats
goods.note: Fodder and the poor's porridge. A penny a modius in 794.

goods.name: Malt
goods.note: Sprouted barley for brewing.

goods.name: Flour
goods.note: Ground at the water mills of the great estates; it keeps far less well than grain.

goods.name: Ship's bread
goods.note: Twice-baked bread for a voyage: about a day's food for 10 men a sack. In 794, 12 wheat loaves of 2 pounds cost a penny.

goods.name: Rhenish wine
goods.season: The new wine after the vintage (Oct-Nov) is cheap; by summer it is dearer
goods.note: The Frisians' great cargo down the Rhine and north: wine in casks, and in fine Tating-ware jugs to drink it from. The Rhine delta (Dorestad, where the Rhine's wine was sold on north and west) counts as making it, at 2 (economy design 2.2).

goods.name: Frankish wine (Seine and Loire)
goods.note: Wine of the Paris basin and the Loire, sold at the Saint-Denis fair and shipped to the English.

goods.name: Wine of Aquitaine
goods.note: Bordeaux's wine, carried up the Atlantic coast to the Irish and the Britons.

goods.name: Mead
goods.note: Honey wine, where honey is plentiful (the Wends and Prussians drink it as others drink ale).

goods.name: Ale
goods.note: Brewed everywhere and soon sour; drunk on board while it lasts. Hopped beer comes later.

goods.name: Bay salt
goods.season: Made in the summer pans; cheapest in autumn
goods.note: Grey salt from the pans of Noirmoutier and the Bay of Bourgneuf: for preserving fish, meat and butter.

goods.name: Droitwich salt
goods.note: Boiled from the brine springs of the Mercian kings' Wich.

goods.name: Rock salt
goods.note: From the Alpine mines (Reichenhall, Hallein), shipped down the Danube and overland; taxed at Raffelstetten.

goods.name: Salt herring
goods.season: Caught in autumn; in demand for Lent
goods.note: The herring shoals of the Sound and the North Sea, salted in barrels (the great Scanian fairs come later).

goods.name: Stockfish
goods.season: Dried on racks over the winter; shipped south in summer
goods.note: Cod air-dried in Lofoten, keeping for years: the great northern trade begins about 1000.

goods.name: Dried fish
goods.note: Ling, pollock and the like, wind-dried along the northern coasts; good ship's food.

goods.name: Eels
goods.note: The Fens paid rents in eels by the thousand.

goods.name: Whale meat and blubber
goods.note: From stranded and hunted whales; a stranding was shared out by law.

goods.name: Cheese
goods.note: The salt-marsh dairies of the Frisian coast.

goods.name: Salt pork and bacon
goods.note: From the oak woods' pannage pigs; ship's food.

goods.name: Honey
goods.note: Wild honey from the forest bee-trees of the east; the only sweetness most people know.

goods.name: Olive oil
goods.note: For the lamps and chrism of the churches; scarce in the north.

goods.name: Pepper
goods.note: From India through the Caliphate; a gift fit for an abbot.

goods.name: Cloves
goods.note: From the Moluccas, by way of the Indian Ocean and Baghdad.

goods.name: Cumin
goods.note: A Mediterranean spice, cheap beside pepper.

goods.name: Sugar
goods.note: Cane sugar from Egypt and al-Andalus: a rare medicine in the north.

goods.name: Almonds
goods.note: Almond milk for fast days in monastic kitchens.

goods.name: Rice
goods.note: Grown in al-Andalus and Sicily; a curiosity in the north.

goods.name: Hops
goods.note: Hop gardens appear on Frankish monastic estates in the 9th century (Corvey's statutes of 822).

goods.name: Cattle
goods.note: Cattle were wealth itself (feoh, fe). They need fodder and water on board: short crossings only.

goods.name: Horses
goods.risk: After 864 the Franks punish selling horses to the Northmen with death (Edict of Pitres).
goods.note: A good stallion was worth a sword or more.

goods.name: Frisian cloth
goods.note: Fine coloured woollens, the 'Frisian cloaks' Charlemagne sent to Harun al-Rashid. Where they were woven (Frisia, Flanders, England) is still argued.

goods.name: Woollen cloth
goods.note: Plain everyday woollens.

goods.name: Wadmal
goods.note: Coarse homespun twill; in Iceland ells of wadmal were money.

goods.name: Fine linen
goods.note: Egyptian linen, for altar cloths and the rich.

goods.name: Silk
goods.note: Byzantine and Islamic silks: vestments, relic wrappings, the trim on a jarl's tunic (silk bands lie in the Birka graves).

goods.name: Silk ribbon and trim
goods.note: Cut into strips and sewn on the best clothes.

goods.name: Cotton cloth
goods.note: Grown in Islamic Spain and the east; almost unknown in the north.

goods.name: Wool
goods.note: England's wool, which the Flemish weavers will come to live on.

goods.name: Hemp
goods.note: For rope and sacking.

goods.name: Woad
goods.note: The blue dye of the north.

goods.name: Madder
goods.note: Root for red dye.

goods.name: Kermes red
goods.note: Scarlet from dried scale insects; the dye of princes' cloaks.

goods.name: Alum
goods.note: The mordant that fixes dyes in wool.

goods.name: Squirrel pelts
goods.season: Winter pelts are the best; bought in spring
goods.note: Grey winter squirrel by the tens of thousands: the commonest fur of the trade.

goods.name: Sable
goods.note: The richest fur of all, from the far north east: the Volga Bulgars sold it on to the Caliphate.

goods.name: Castoreum
goods.note: Beaver musk: a medicine and a base for perfume.

goods.name: Fox pelts
goods.note: Red fox, and the white and blue arctic fox of the far north.

goods.name: Bear skins
goods.note: Brown bear from the forests; white bear skins from Greenland after 985 were a gift for kings.

goods.name: Reindeer hides
goods.note: Part of the tribute the Sami paid the northern chieftains.

goods.name: Walrus-hide rope
goods.note: Ohthere told King Alfred the walrus's hide makes the best ship-ropes.

goods.name: Walrus ivory
goods.note: Ohthere brought walrus tusks to King Alfred; carved into croziers, combs and gaming pieces.

goods.name: Narwhal tusk
goods.note: Sold as unicorn's horn; for royal and church treasuries.

goods.name: Elephant ivory
goods.note: African ivory for book covers and reliquaries of the court workshops.

goods.name: Antler
goods.note: Red deer and reindeer antler for the comb-makers of Ribe and Hedeby.

goods.name: Horn
goods.note: Cattle horn for drinking horns, spoons and lantern panes.

goods.name: Whalebone
goods.note: For carved plaques and gaming pieces.

goods.name: Mayen quernstones
goods.note: Hand-mills of Eifel lava from Mayen, carried down the Rhine: found in nearly every house from Dorestad to Birka.

goods.name: Millstones
goods.note: Great stones for the water mills of estates and abbeys; a heavy cargo.

goods.name: Whetstones
goods.note: Schist hones from the quarries of Eidsborg in Telemark, shipped out through Kaupang.

goods.name: Soapstone pots
goods.note: Cooking pots, lamps and spindle whorls carved from steatite.

goods.name: Rhenish pottery
goods.note: Badorf and Mayen storage jars and jugs, by the shipload to the coast.

goods.name: Tating-ware jugs
goods.note: Black jugs laid with tin foil crosses: fine tableware for serving wine; found from Dorestad to Birka.

goods.name: Pingsdorf ware
goods.note: Red-painted Rhenish ware that follows Badorf.

goods.name: Ipswich ware
goods.note: The first wheel-thrown pottery of England since the Romans, from the kilns of Gipeswic.

goods.name: Glass vessels
goods.note: Funnel beakers and claw beakers from the Rhenish glasshouses; for feasting in a hall. Fragile.

goods.name: Glass beads
goods.note: Made in the bead workshops of Ribe and Hedeby from imported raw glass.

goods.name: Raw glass and tesserae
goods.note: Old mosaic cubes and broken glass, melted down for beads.

goods.name: Carnelian and crystal beads
goods.note: Indian and Persian stone beads that came north with the silver of the Caliphate.

goods.name: Amber
goods.season: Gathered on the beaches after the autumn storms
goods.note: Baltic amber from the Samland coast; worked into beads and amulets at Ribe and Hedeby.

goods.name: Jet
goods.note: Whitby jet, which Bede praises; York's jet-workers flourish in the 10th century.

goods.name: Pearls
goods.note: Gulf pearls; and the river pearls of Scotland.

goods.name: Bar iron
goods.note: Bog iron smelted in the forests (the Veluwe's furnaces among the biggest) and traded in standard bars.

goods.name: Iron tools
goods.note: Axes, knives, sickles, shears, tongs.

goods.name: Nails and ship rivets
goods.note: Clench nails for clinker planking.

goods.name: Crucible steel
goods.note: (?) High-carbon steel from Persia and Central Asia, perhaps the stuff of the best Ulfberht blades; how it travelled is argued.

goods.name: Copper
goods.note: The Rammelsberg mines in the Harz open in 968.

goods.name: Brass
goods.note: Rhenish and Mosan brass, melted down in the north for oval brooches.

goods.name: Tin
goods.note: Cornish tin, for bronze and pewter (and the foil on Tating jugs).

goods.name: Lead
goods.note: For church roofs and gutters: Charlemagne asked Offa for lead.

goods.name: Quicksilver
goods.note: From Almaden; for fire-gilding brooches and church metalwork.

goods.name: Swords
goods.risk: Frankish law forbids selling arms out of the realm: byrnies (Herstal 779), weapons and mail to the Slavs and Avars (Thionville 805); after 864, death for selling arms or horses to the Northmen (Pitres). Frankish officers search ships.
goods.note: 7 shillings with its scabbard in the Ripuarian law. Frankish blades were wanted from Ireland to the Volga; the Rus sold them on in the east.

goods.name: Ulfberht sword blades
goods.note: Unhilted blades signed ULFBERHT, from about 800: hilted in the north.

goods.name: Spearheads
goods.risk: As swords: Frankish arms laws (winged Frankish spearheads especially).

goods.name: Battle axes
goods.risk: Arms: as swords where the Franks rule.

goods.name: Mail byrnies
goods.risk: No byrnie may be sold out of the Frankish realm (Herstal 779); merchants caught lose all they carry (Thionville 805).
goods.note: 12 shillings in the Ripuarian law: a fortune.

goods.name: Helmets
goods.note: 6 shillings in the Ripuarian law.

goods.name: Shields
goods.note: Lime-wood boards, hide-faced, with an iron boss. A shield and spear: 2 shillings.

goods.name: Captives
goods.risk: The Church forbids selling Christians to pagans, Jews or Saracens; the Franks forbid selling slaves out of the realm. Pagan Slavs were sold lawfully through Verdun to Spain. Christian lands abhor it; Norse and Rus markets don't care. Freeing captives by ransom is a good deed.
goods.note: People: each needs food and water like a crewman. Shown as a lot in the market like any other.

goods.name: Books
goods.note: Gospel books, psalters, sacramentaries and law books, copied in the scriptoria of Wearmouth-Jarrow, Tours, Corbie and the court school; new churches in Saxony and Frisia need them.

goods.name: Parchment
goods.note: Calf and sheep skin; a big book takes a whole herd.

goods.name: Papyrus
goods.note: Egyptian papyrus, still used by the papal chancery till the mid 11th century.

goods.name: Pigments and ink
goods.note: Orpiment, vermilion, and lapis lazuli from Afghanistan for the illuminators.

goods.name: Frankincense
goods.note: Arabian incense for the churches.

goods.name: Relics
goods.risk: Buying or selling holy relics is simony; stealing them is sacrilege, though thieves' tales were told as miracles.
goods.note: Saints' bones from Rome's catacombs, wanted by every new church.

goods.name: Church plate
goods.risk: Plate looted from churches marks its seller.
goods.note: Silver chalices and patens.

goods.name: Brooches
goods.note: Oval brooches, cast in the towns' workshops by the hundred.

goods.name: Musk
goods.note: From the Tibetan musk deer, by the silk roads.

goods.name: Oak timber
goods.note: For ships and halls; the treeless Frisian coast and the northern islands need it all.

goods.name: Yew staves
goods.note: Bow wood.

goods.name: Pine tar
goods.note: For caulking and preserving a ship's timbers and ropes.

goods.name: Rope
goods.note: Bast and hemp rope.

goods.name: Sailcloth
goods.note: Close-woven wool, greased against the wind.

goods.name: Potash
goods.note: Wood ash for the glassmakers and soap boilers.

goods.name: Hunting falcons
goods.season: Taken from the nest in summer
goods.note: Gyrfalcons and peregrines: gifts between kings, from Norway and later Iceland and Greenland.

goods.name: Hounds
goods.note: Hunting dogs, sent as gifts.

goods.name: Feathers
goods.note: Bedding; part of the Sami tribute.

goods.name: Whale oil
goods.note: Train oil for lamps and dressing leather.

goods.name: Beeswax
goods.note: Candles for every altar: the Church's endless want.

goods.name: Sulphur
goods.note: From Iceland's hot grounds, for medicine and bleaching.
